summaries.summary: Twitter generates nearly 500 million tweets per day, and its short, informal, metadata-rich, grammatically irregular data poses interesting NLP challenges and use cases.
Task 1 of WASSA-2017 BIBREF0 asks for emotion intensity of anger, fear, joy, sadness from tweets, and this paper describes its approach and experiments.
Preprocessing uses tweetokenize, replaces Twitter-specific features with USERNAME, PHONENUMBER, NUMBER, URL and TIME, splits emoji sequences, and lowercases tokens.

Sentiment or emotion tasks use affect, opinion, sentiment, sense and emotion lexicons, low dimensional vectors, and traditional NLP features like word N-grams, character N-grams, Part-Of-Speech N-grams and word clusters.

Feature extraction is implemented in the Python program EmoInt as fourteen independent feature extractors with baseline features, additional extractors and bi-gram support, grouped into 3 major categories.

Lexicon Features include AFINN BIBREF3, Bing Liu BIBREF4, +/-EffectWordNet BIBREF5, NRC Affect Intensity BIBREF6, NRC Word-Emotion Association Lexicon BIBREF7, Expanded NRC Word-Emotion Association Lexicon BIBREF8, NRC Hashtag Emotion Lexicon BIBREF9, NRC Hashtag Sentiment Lexicon and Sentiment140 Lexicon BIBREF10, SentiWordNet BIBREF11, negation lexicons and SentiStrength BIBREF12.

Word Vectors integrate 200-dimensional GloVe embeddings trained on 2 Billion tweets, Edinburgh embeddings BIBREF14, and Emoji embeddings BIBREF16, with tweet embeddings formed by averaging word vectors.
Syntactic Features integrate Word N-grams, Part-Of-Speech N-grams BIBREF17 and Brown Cluster N-grams BIBREF18 obtained using TweetNLP project.
The final feature vector concatenates individual features, and scaling is not required for gradient boosted trees but standard scaling may benefit neural networks.
A total of fourteen different feature extractors have been implemented, each individually enabled or disabled to extract features from a given tweet.

Train and dev sets were merged for 10-fold cross validation, predictions averaged across folds, and sklearn BIBREF20 regressors evaluated using Pearson's Correlation Coefficient and Spearman's rank-order correlation.

Grid search through scikit-Learn over shuffled training subsets used stratified 10-fold cross validation and optimized Pearson's Correlation score, with best results from AdaBoost meta regressor with XGBoost BIBREF21, 1000 estimators and 0.1 learning rate.

Syntax features were dropped, Emoji embeddings BIBREF16 outperformed plain GloVe and Edinburgh embeddings, the official submission ranked 3 overall and 2 on scores greater than or equal to 0.5, and averaging the top 2 models outperformed individual models.

Feature importance is assessed by decision-node depth across randomized trees, and +/-EffectWordNet BIBREF5, NRC Hashtag Sentiment Lexicon, Sentiment140 Lexicon BIBREF10 and NRC Hashtag Emotion Lexicon BIBREF9 play the most important role.
Mostly lexicon based features cause difficulties with overall sentiment, sarcastic tweets, deeper emotion and sentiment, very short sentences, and amplifying or vanishing intensity signals.

The paper studies affect lexicons and word embeddings for emotional intensity in tweets and open-sources EmoInt, a light-weight affect computing framework with feature extractors and ensemble scripts.
Sentence embeddings may resolve context problems, generic features may apply to other social media affective computing tasks, and benchmarking run-time performance may support real-world deployment.
The authors thank the organizers of the WASSA-2017 Shared Task on Emotion Intensity for data, guidelines and timely support.
